notes.summary: Environment gives about 1 question per paper, sometimes 2. Past papers ask about protected areas and treaties, pollution and global warming, and ecosystem basics (food chains, the 10% law, who coined which term). Learn national parks with their state and famous animal, and treaties with their year and purpose.

concepts.title: Ecology and ecosystems
concepts.body:
• Ernst Haeckel coined 'ecology' (1866). A.G. Tansley coined 'ecosystem' (1935). Eugene P. Odum is called the father of modern ecology; he treated the ecosystem as the basic unit of ecology.
  • Autecology studies one species; synecology studies communities of many species.
  • Levels: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere.
  • Biotic parts: producers (green plants), consumers (primary: herbivores; secondary and tertiary: carnivores), decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Abiotic parts: light, water, soil, air, temperature.
  • Food chain: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle. Linked chains make a food web.
  • Lindeman's 10% law (1942): only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level. So chains rarely have more than 4 or 5 links.
  • Ecological pyramids: the energy pyramid is always upright. The pyramid of numbers is inverted for a single tree with many insects; the pyramid of biomass is inverted in the sea.
  • Biomagnification: poisons like DDT and mercury build up at higher trophic levels.

concepts.title: Succession, biomes and hotspots
concepts.body:
• Ecological succession: gradual change in a community. Primary succession starts on bare rock (pioneers: lichens); secondary succession starts where soil exists (after fire or farming). It ends in a stable climax community.
  • Ecotone: a transition zone between two ecosystems (like a mangrove between land and sea). Niche: a species' role in its habitat.
  • Keystone species have a large effect on their ecosystem (tiger, fig tree). Indicator species show environmental health (lichens are sensitive to sulphur dioxide). Flagship species draw public support (tiger, panda).
  • Biomes: tropical rainforests have the richest biodiversity; others are deserts, grasslands, taiga (coniferous) and tundra.
  • India is one of 17 megadiverse countries and has parts of 4 of the world's biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).
  • Afforestation reduces floods and soil erosion and keeps the ecosystem in balance.

concepts.title: Protected areas
concepts.body:
• National park: strict protection; no grazing or private rights. Wildlife sanctuary: some human activity allowed. Conservation and community reserves were added in 2002.
  • Biosphere reserve: core, buffer and transition zones (UNESCO Man and the Biosphere programme, 1971). India's first: Nilgiri (1986).
  • India's first national park: Hailey National Park (1936), now Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand). Largest national park: Hemis (Ladakh). Largest tiger reserve: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (Andhra Pradesh).
  • Ramsar sites (wetlands of international importance): India's first two (1981) were Chilika (Odisha) and Keoladeo (Rajasthan). The Sundarbans is India's largest Ramsar site. The number rises each year.

concepts.title: Pollution
concepts.body:
• Air pollutants: carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10), ground-level ozone, lead. India's Air Quality Index (2014) has six categories from good to severe.
  • Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form acids; rain with pH below about 5.6. It damages marble ('stone cancer' at the Taj Mahal).
  • Smog: classical smog (smoke and fog, London type) and photochemical smog (ozone, PAN; sunny traffic-heavy cities).
  • Water: high BOD (biological oxygen demand) means more organic pollution. Eutrophication: nitrates and phosphates cause algal blooms that use up oxygen.
  • Noise: measured in decibels; long exposure above about 80 dB harms hearing.
  • Disasters: Bhopal gas leak (methyl isocyanate, December 1984); Chernobyl nuclear accident (1986); Fukushima (2011).
  • India banned many single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022.

concepts.title: Climate change and the ozone layer
concepts.body:
• Greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and water vapour. They trap heat and cause global warming, the long-term rise in Earth's surface temperature since pre-industrial times.
  • IPCC (1988, set up by UNEP and WMO) assesses climate science.
  • The ozone layer is in the stratosphere and blocks ultraviolet rays. CFCs (from old fridges, ACs, sprays) are the main cause of ozone depletion; the 'ozone hole' forms over Antarctica. Ozone is measured in Dobson units.
  • India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) has eight missions, including the National Solar Mission and the Green India Mission.
  • At COP26 (2021) India announced a target of net zero by 2070.
  • Carbon sequestration stores carbon (forests, oceans, soil); a carbon credit allows one tonne of CO2 to be emitted.

varieties.name: Ecology and ecosystems
varieties.how: Learn who coined which term, the trophic levels, and the 10% law. For 10% questions, divide by 10 for each step up.

example.q: Producers trap 20,000 J. By the 10% law, how much reaches secondary consumers?
steps: Secondary consumers get 10% of that: 200 J.

varieties.name: Biodiversity and wildlife
varieties.how: Learn the Red List order and a few Indian species in each category, plus project names with years.

example.q: Which endemic owl of central India was moved to Endangered on the IUCN Red List in 2018?
steps: The bird was thought extinct until it was found again in 1997.
It is the forest owlet, earlier Critically Endangered.

varieties.name: National parks and protected areas
varieties.how: Learn park, state and signature animal as a set. Lions only in Gir; rhinos in Kaziranga; hangul in Dachigam; sangai in Keibul Lamjao.

example.q: Gir National Park is famous for which animal?
steps: It is the only wild home of the Asiatic lion.

varieties.name: Pollution and climate change
varieties.how: Link each pollutant to its source and effect. For pollution diseases, learn the metal or chemical behind each.

example.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning from:
steps: The disease broke out in Minamata, Japan.
Factory waste put mercury into fish eaten by people.

varieties.name: Environmental conventions and bodies
varieties.how: Learn each treaty's year and one-word purpose: Ramsar wetlands, Montreal ozone, Kyoto emissions, Basel waste, Cartagena GMOs.

example.q: Which agreement protects the ozone layer?
steps: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances.

varieties.name: Environmental laws and movements
varieties.how: Learn each Act with its year and trigger, and each movement with place, year and leader.

example.q: The Environment (Protection) Act was passed in 1986 after which event?
steps: It is an umbrella law passed soon after a major industrial disaster.
That disaster was the Bhopal gas leak of December 1984.

tips: Red List order: 'Every Elephant Can't Easily Visit New Lands' gives Extinct, Extinct in Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern.
10% law: each step up the food chain, drop one zero.
Treaty hooks: Ramsar wetlands (1971), Montreal ozone (1987), Kyoto carbon (1997), Paris 1.5 °C (2015).
Pollution diseases: Minamata mercury (M-M), Itai-itai cadmium, blue baby nitrate.
Water Act 1974 comes before the Air Act 1981; EPA 1986 follows Bhopal 1984.
Corbett (Hailey, 1936) was India's first national park; Nilgiri (1986) was the first biosphere reserve.
traps: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere; ground-level ozone is a pollutant.
Montreal Protocol is about the ozone layer, not climate; Kyoto and Paris are about climate.
A national park is stricter than a wildlife sanctuary.
The energy pyramid is never inverted, but number and biomass pyramids can be.

questions.q: Gir National Park is famous for which animal?
questions.solution:
Gir National Park and the surrounding Gir forest region of Gujarat form the only wild home of the Asiatic lion.
Memory hook: Gir — 'Gir-r-r' is the lion's roar.

questions.q: In an ecosystem, green plants are called:
questions.solution:
Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers.
Memory hook: Plants Produce.

questions.q: Which gas is mainly responsible for depletion of the ozone layer?
questions.solution:
CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere, which breaks down ozone. They were used in fridges and sprays.
Memory hook: Chlorine from CFCs 'chews' ozone.

questions.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning from:
questions.solution:
Minamata disease (Japan) was caused by mercury in fish from polluted water. Itai-itai is due to cadmium.
Memory hook: Minamata = Mercury.

questions.q: Which was the first national park of India?
questions.solution:
Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand) was set up in 1936 as Hailey National Park — India's first. Project Tiger was launched here in 1973.
Memory hook: Corbett: first park, first Project Tiger reserve.

questions.q: According to Lindeman's 10% law, if producers trap 20,000 J of energy, how much will reach the secondary consumers?
questions.solution:
Primary consumers get 10% of 20,000 = 2,000 J. Secondary consumers get 10% of 2,000 = 200 J.
Memory hook: Drop one zero at each step up the pyramid.

questions.q: Which international agreement is specifically aimed at protecting the ozone layer?
questions.solution:
The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs. Kyoto and Paris deal with greenhouse gases; Ramsar with wetlands.
Memory hook: 'O' in Ozone — the 'O' in mOntreal.

questions.q: The Environment (Protection) Act of India was passed in 1986 after which disaster?
questions.solution:
The Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984, methyl isocyanate leak from Union Carbide) led to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
Memory hook: Bhopal '84 → Act '86.
